Issued at 230 PM CDT Thu Jul 30 2026

Southwesterly flow is found over the northern Plains this 
afternoon as a shortwave traverses the upper level ridge exiting
the region to the east. With the passage of this shortwave, 
showers and thunderstorms have developed across much of western 
and central North Dakota today, mostly along the associated 
surface cold front slowly making its way southeast across the 
forecast area. With the greater access to the Gulf moisture 
plume that this pattern allows, dewpoints are expected to rise 
well into the mid 60s to mid 70s this afternoon, highest across 
the south central. With this contributing to model MUCAPE values
peaking well into the 1500 to 2500 J/KG range, and with the 
broad synoptic lift accentuated by 850mb jet dynamics late this 
afternoon and evening, at least a few stronger to marginally 
severe thunderstorms will be possible today, though they will 
need to overcome a weak 850-900mb CAP. The overall lack of shear
across the area, with model 0-6KM values peaking only around 15
to 25 knots, is expected to keep any stronger storms fairly 
transient. As of the latest forecast cycles, short term CAMs 
dial into the stronger storm potential over the southwest late 
this afternoon, where the influence of the mid level jet is 
expected to be greatest, and where a weak surface low anchored 
to the cold front is expected to cut across before moving into 
South Dakota. Of note today is the potential for landspouts to 
develop along the slow moving cold front, with global models 
advertising enhanced surface vorticity along this boundary in 
the mid afternoon through the early evening. The area to watch 
would be over south central into southeastern North Dakota, 
including the James River Valley, where this surface vorticity 
is both maximized and potentially further enhanced by subsequent
outflow boundary interactions from decaying storms earlier in 
the day. SPC has placed much of the forecast area along and 
south of Highway 200 into a Marginal (level 1 of 5) Risk for 
isolated severe thunderstorms this afternoon. Regarding 
potential hazards we will continue to advertise large hail up to
the size of quarters, and wind gusts up to 60 MPH, while also 
mentioning the expectation for locally heavy rainfall where and
when thunderstorms develop. High PWATs in the 1.5 to 2.0
range and warm rain processes have already contributed to
rainfall totals of 1.5 to 2.5 inches across portions of the
northern James River Valley this morning, where storms were
fairly short lived. The developing storms this afternoon have 
been fairly stationary so far, which means this heavy rainfall 
may linger over an area for a while. We will need to monitor for
potential flooding through this afternoon and evening, though 
CAMs continue to advertise the gradual acceleration of this 
system out of the forecast area through the late afternoon and 
evening.

Otherwise, the main story through the remainder of the week is 
going to be the return of warmer temperatures and drier 
conditions as a transient upper level ridge slides across the 
northern Plains. While lingering zonal flow and a weak shortwave
could promote some scattered storms will be possible over the 
northwest on Friday, the shift toward northwesterly flow will 
preclude any notable precipitation through the weekend. Highs 
each day are expected to increase, from being broadly in the 80s
this afternoon, into the 80s and 90s on Friday, and back into 
the 90s and 100s Saturday and Sunday. Despite the lower 
dewpoints expected across the forecast area this weekend, some 
consideration for potential heat headlines must be given over 
the next few forecast cycles, especially as the contribution of 
short-term CAMs to the ensemble increases, and as the potential 
for compressive heating ahead of a weak cold front late Saturday
through Sunday may drive temperatures across portions of the 
south central evening well into the upper end of the model 
spread. 

Of note during this period is the potential for near critical 
to critical fire weather conditions across portions of western 
North Dakota starting Sunday. The passage of the aforementioned 
weak cold front Saturday night through Sunday, then the passage 
of a stronger cold front Sunday through Monday, is expected to 
promote breezy winds in the afternoon and evening hours. With 
mostly prevailing dry conditions expected through this period, 
though the passage of the stronger cold front Sunday through 
Monday may promote at least low chances for showers and storms 
across much of western and central North Dakota, and with fuels 
across much of western and especially south central North Dakota
having started to cure over the past few weeks, we will need to
monitor trends over the next few days due to fire weather 
concerns.
